extracted.intended_audience: scholars/translators of ancient mathematics; historians of mathematics; classical philologists; mathematicians studying Archimedes' terminology
extracted.subtask_description: A glossary-style exposition of the technical Greek vocabulary Archimedes (and related authors) use for geometric objects, constructions, motions and algebraic operations, with examples of idiomatic phrases and syntactic usage. Intended to guide translation and interpretation of classical geometric texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage of δύνασθαι / δυνάμει
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on the Greek verb for 'to be able': when δύνασθαι is used (sometimes as δυνάμει) and when it is used alone it is followed by the accusative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example idiom: 'the square (on a straight line) is equal to the rectangle contained by... is (εὐθεῖα) ἴσον δύναται τῷ περιεχομένῳ' — shows that δύναται may govern an accusative. Pay attention to this construction in translating modal statements of possibility/ability in geometric propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gnomon and breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Gnomon = γνώμων; its breadth = πλάτος; the breadth refers to the breadth of each end of the gnomon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: 'γνώμων πλάτος ἔχων ἴσον τῷ BI' (a gnomon whose breadth is equal to BI) and comparative forms 'πλάτος ἑνὶ τμάματι μείζον' (breadth greater by one segment). Useful when translating iterative constructions involving gnomons and their widths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygon terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Polygons: πολύγωνον; equilateral polygon ἰσόπλευρον; polygon with an even number of sides/angles ἀρτιόπλευρον or ἀρτιόγωνον; special phrasings for polygons with all sides equal except a base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'πολύγωνον ἰσόπλευρον' for an equilateral polygon; 'τὰς πλευρὰς ἴσας καὶ ἀρτίους' to indicate sides equal and even in number. Also terms for polygons measured by four (regular polygon whose number of sides is measured by four) and high-order names like χιλιάγωνον (a chiliagon). Watch for idiomatic qualifiers describing which side(s) are excluded ('χωρὶς τῆς βάσεως').

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines subtending polygon sides
rubrics_metrics.description: The straight line subtending two sides (joining angles next but one) and lines subtending one less than half the number of sides have specific phrasings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: 'αἱ ὑπὸ δύο πλευρὰς ὑποτείνουσαι' and 'ὑποτείνουσα τὰς μιᾷ ἐλάσσονας τῶν ἡμίσεων.' Important for describing diagonals and special chords in inscribed/circumscribed polygon discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle vocabulary and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle = κύκλος; circumference/arc = περιφέρεια (used both for whole circumference and a circular arc); perimeter also appears as περίμετρος (less common in Archimedes). Radius expressed as ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου; diameter διάμετρος; chord phrases include ἡ ἐμπεσοῦσα or ἡ ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ἡ BA περιφέρεια' for arc BA; 'ὁ κύκλος ὃ ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου ἂ ΘΕ' for 'the circle whose radius is ΘE'; 'περὶ διάμετρον τὴν AE κύκλος' for 'circle on AE as diameter.' Translate περιφέρεια contextually as arc or whole circumference. Note Archimedes' variable use of περίμετρος in other treatises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle segments, semicircles and sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment = τμῆμα κύκλου; semicircle = ἡμικύκλιον; sector = τομεύς or, when needed to distinguish from a solid sector, ἐπίπεδος τομεὺς κύκλου. The 'angle of the semicircle' denotes the right angle contained by the diameter and the arc (or tangent) at its extremity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: 'τὸ τμῆμα ἔλασσον ἡμικυκλίον ὃ ἀποτέμνει τὴν AB' for a segment less than a semicircle cut off by AB. Sectors may be spoken of as having a 'side' equal to a radius (πλευρά). Where precise distinction is required, use ἐπίπεδος τομεύς for plane sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribed and circumscribed polygons & leftover parts
rubrics_metrics.description: To inscribe = ἐγγράφειν/ἐγγεγράφθω; to circumscribe = περιγράφειν/περιγεγράφθω/περιγεγραμμένος. Spaces between polygon and circle have many names: περιλειπόμενα τμήματα, τὰ περιλειπόμενα σχήματα, τὰ περιλείμματα, τὰ ἀπολείμματα.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example phrase: 'ἐπὶ τῆς AT πολύγωνον ἐγγεγράφθω εἰς τὸ ΑΒΓ τμῆμα' (let a polygon be inscribed on AT in the segment ABT). Use the appropriate Greek term to indicate whether the polygon is inscribed in a circle, a sector, or a segment, and use one of the several words for 'remainder' depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere terminology and spherical parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sphere = σφαῖρα; centre = κέντρον; radius = ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου; hemisphere = ἡμισφαίριον; segments τμήματα σφαιρικά; curved surface = ἐπιφάνεια; base = βάσις, vertex = κορυφή, height = ὕψος.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: 'τὸ κατὰ τὸ Γ' τμῆμα τῆς σφαίρας' for a segment at a point, and adjectival uses like 'ἐπιφάνεια' to denote spherical surface. Note comparative statements: 'τὸ ἡμισφαίριον μεῖζόν ἐστι τῶν...'. Useful for translating arguments about maximal surfaces or segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism and pyramid vocabulary & surface phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Prism = πρῖσμα; pyramid = πυραμίς. Describing a prism/pyramid on a rectilinear base uses ἀναγράφειν ἀπό (e.g., ἀναγεγράφθω ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐθυγράμμου πρῖσμα). 'Surface' excluding bases requires qualifying phrases (e.g., ἡ ἐπιφάνεια τοῦ πρίσματος ἡ ἐκ τῶν παραλληλογράμμων συγκειμένη).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ἡ ἐπιφάνεια χωρὶς τῆς βάσεως' for surface excluding the base; 'τὰ περιέχοντα τρίγωνα τὴν πυραμίδα' to indicate the triangular faces bounding a pyramid. Keep qualifiers when translating to indicate exclusion/inclusion of bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cones: types, parts and special terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes commonly calls right cones 'isosceles cones' (κῶνος ἰσοσκελής) though he sometimes uses ὀρθός; oblique circular cones appear as 'scalene cone' (κῶνος σκαληνός) in Apollonius. Usual parts: vertex κορυφή, base βάσις, axis ἄξων, height ὕψος, generator called a 'side' πλευρά. Frustum has no special one-word name; segment of cone = ἀπότμαμα κώνου; axis (ἄξων) also used as line joining vertices in special contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'κωνικὴ ἐπιφάνεια ἡ μεταξὺ τῶν ΑΔΒ' for conical surface between generators AD and AB. 'ἀπότμαμα κώνου' denotes the portion cut off towards the vertex by a plane making an elliptic (not circular) section. Translate 'generator' as πλευρά in Archimedean contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid rhombus (double cone) vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid rhombus = ῥόμβος στερεός, defined as the figure made up of two cones with a common base, vertices on opposite sides and axes in one straight line. The two cones are called the cones bounding the rhombus (κῶνοι οἱ περιέχοντες τὸν ῥόμβον).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrasing useful when translating compound solids: 'ῥόμβος ἐξ ἰσοσκελῶν κώνων συγκείμενος' to indicate the rhombus composed of isosceles cones. Maintain the paired-cone imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cylinder terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Right cylinder = κύλινδρος ὀρθός; parts: base βάσις (either base ἡ ἑτέρα βάσις), axis ἄξων, height ὕψος, generator πλευρά. Phrases for cylindrical surface between generators and surface adjacent to a circumference are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ἡ ἀποτεμνομένη κυλινδρικὴ ἐπιφάνεια ὑπὸ τῶν AT, ΒΔ' for the cylindrical surface cut off by generators AT and BD. For frustums of cylinders (τόμος κυλίνδρον) note the axis joins centres of the two (elliptic) sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conic sections vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: General name κωνικὰ στοιχεῖα / τὰ κωνικά. A parabola = (section of) right-angled cone ὀρθογωνίου κώνου τομή; hyperbola = section of obtuse-angled cone; ellipse = section of acute-angled cone. Archimedes uses διάμετροι (diameters) in place of our 'axes' for conics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangent is ἐπιψαύουσα or ἐφαπτομένη. Note that 'axis' as ἄξων is not used for conics; instead διάμετρος refers to diameters of the complete conic. Render such terms with care to avoid imposing later conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola-specific terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Axis of complete parabola is called a diameter (διάμετρος); other diameters are lines parallel to it. A 'segment' of a parabola is τμῆμα bounded by a straight line and a section of a right-angled cone. The diameter of a segment is the line bisecting all chords drawn parallel to its base. Frustum (portion between two parallel chords) = τόμος with lesser and greater bases (ἐλάσσων and μείζων βάσις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes' 'latus rectum' corresponds to 'the line which is double of the line drawn as far as the axis' (διπλασία τᾶς μέχρι τοῦ ἄξονος). He also uses a phrase equivalent to 'parameter' (παρ᾽ ἃν δυνάνται...) describing the rectangle relation between ordinates and abscissas. Render technical relations (squares of ordinates equal to rectangles applied to a fixed line) in line with Archimedean phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola and asymptotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymptotes are described as 'the lines (approaching) nearest to the section of the obtuse-angled cone' (αἱ ἔγγιστα τᾶς τοῦ ἀμβλυγωνίου κώνου τομάς). Archimedes does not commonly use 'centre' the way later authors do; the point at which the nearest lines meet is called τὸ κέντρον in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate ἔγγιστα as 'lines nearest to the section' or 'asymptotes' depending on context; note Archimedes' geometric origin language rather than the later analytic conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse: diameters and conjugate axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Major and minor axes = μείζων and ἐλάσσων διάμετρος. One axis is called conjugate (συζυγής) to the other. The rectangle contained by the diameters (axes) is τὸ περιεχόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν διαμέτρων.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example phrase: 'Ν εὐθεῖα ἴσα ἔστω τῷ ἡμισείᾳ τῆς ἑτέρας διαμέτρου, ἃ ἐστι συζυγὴς τῷ ΑΒ.' Use συζυγής where conjugacy between axes is implied; preserve 'διάμετρος' as Archimedes' term for axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conoids and spheroids vocabulary and segment axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Conoid = κωνοειδές (paraboloid/hyperboloid of revolution as qualifiers added); spheroid = σφαιροειδές. Archimedes defines genesis by revolution of a section about a fixed diameter; he uses qualifiers like ὀρθογώνιον (right-angled) or ἀμβλυγώνιον (obtuse-angled) transferred from the conic to the solid. Vertex κορυφή, axis ἄξων, segment base defined as the plane figure included by the section, and special rules for defining the axis of a segment differ for paraboloid/hyperboloid/spheroid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for paraboloid segment the axis is 'the straight line cut off within the segment from the line drawn through the vertex of the segment parallel to the axis of the conoid.' For hyperboloid the axis is cut off from the line through the segment vertex and the vertex of the enveloping cone. Note Archimedes' practice of defining enveloping cones (κῶνον ἰσοσκελέα περιλαψονται) and calling the cone 'enveloping' (περιέχων τὸ κωνοειδές).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special spheroid vocabulary (oblony/flat) and centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of spheroids: oblony (παραμακὲς σφαιροειδές) when revolved about the greater diameter; flat (ἐπιπλατὺ σφαιροειδές) when revolved about the lesser. The centre of a spheroid is the midpoint of the axis (τὸ μέσον τοῦ ἄξονος).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the qualifiers as Archimedes does to reflect which diameter is used for revolution. Note Archimedes does not always use 'centre' for hyperboloid; he may call the vertex of the enveloping cone the centre in hyperboloid contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral (ἕλικα) construction vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: if a straight line turns uniformly about one fixed extremity while a point moves uniformly along the line from that extremity, the point describes a spiral in the plane. Terms: origin ἀρχὰ τᾶς ἕλικος; initial line ἀρχὰ τᾶς περιφορᾶς; first/second distances εὐθεῖα πρώτα/δευτέρα; first area χωρίον πρῶτον; first circle κύκλος πρῶτος; 'turns' of the spiral ἕλικες.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes enumerates areas added per turn and relates circles with radii equal to integer multiples of the 'first distance.' Translate temporal phrases ('in the time in which...') carefully: χρόνοι denotes the times in which the point moved. Directions along a radius vector are 'forward' τὰ προαγούμενα and 'backward' τὰ ἑπόμενα.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent/contact vocabulary and verb distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs for meeting/touching and tangency: ἅπτομαι is broadly 'to meet' and not strictly 'to touch'; to touch a curve/surface is ἐφάπτεσθαι or ἐπιψαύειν (with gen.). Tangent (line) = ἐφαπτομένη or ἐπιψαύουσα; tangent plane = ἐπιψαῦον ἐπίπεδον; the point of contact = ἡ ἀφη (point may be described by κατά + acc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ἅπτομαι (meet/lie on) from ἐπιψαύειν/ἐφάπτεσθαι (touch without cutting). Phrases: 'τὰ ἐπιψαύοντα ἐπίπεδα... καθ᾽ ἕν μόνον ἁπτόνται σαμεῖον' (tangent planes meet the spheroid's surface at one point only). Be attentive to which verb is used to infer geometric relation (meeting vs. tangency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary for constructions (verbs and imperatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich set of verbs and idioms for drawing and constructing: ἄγω/διάγω (draw/lead), xarayw (harshly transcribed here; used for drawing ordinates), προσάγω (draw to meet), προσβάλλω, προσπίπτω, ἐκβάλλω (produce), πρόσκειμαι (be added), and the passive/imperative forms commonly used to express 'let it be made' (perfect imperative passive: γεγονέτω, ἔστω, κείσθω).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common formulae: 'κείσθω τῷ Δ ἴσον τὸ BY' (let BY be made equal to Δ), 'ἤχθω' (let it be drawn), 'ἐκβεβλήσθωσαν' (let them be produced). Also the passive imperative of νοέω (νοείσθω) for 'let it be conceived.' Retain the imperative passive style when rendering classical construction commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions: idioms for supposition and participles
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions often use 'suppose' via νοεῖσθω/νοείσθω, the perfect/passive imperatives, the aorist/perfect participle forms, and the absolute genitive of the passive participle (εὑρεθέντος δή etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'νοείσθω ἡ σφαῖρα τετμημένη' (let the sphere be conceived cut), 'γεγονέτω' (let it be done). When translating, preserve the procedural and hypothetical tone by rendering these imperatives and particples appropriately (e.g., 'let it be supposed', 'let there be drawn').

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary for addition and sums of magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: To add: προστίθημι, with passive πρόσκειμαι; to be added together: συντίθεσθαι. Sums for two magnitudes: συναμφότερος. 'Plus' expressed with μετά (with gen.), σύν, τε, καί. 'Sum of areas' and 'sum of circles' have idiomatic plural expressions ('οἱ πάντες κύκλοι' for sum of all circles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: 'ἡ το ton ἀμφοτέραις ταῖς ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου' for 'line equal to both radii'; 'σύν'/'μετά' with genitive to express addition. Use συναμφότερος for the combined magnitude of two items. For iterative addition Archimedean idioms like ἐπισυντιθέμενον (added repeatedly) appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary for subtraction and differences
rubrics_metrics.description: To subtract: ἀφαιρεῖν; to indicate terms common to each side: κοινά; remainder: λοιπός; difference/excess: ὑπεροχή (or ᾧ μείζων ἐστί...), opposite 'to be lacking' λείπεται. Excesses may be described quantitatively ('ίσον μιᾳ ὑπεροχᾳ', 'δυσὶν ὑπεροχαῖς').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical constructions: 'κοινὸν ἀφῃρήσθω τὸ χωρίον' (let the common area be subtracted), 'ᾧ δὴ ὑπερέχει τὰ εἰρημένα τρίγωνα' to express the difference by which one set exceeds another. Maintain these idioms when rendering algebraic relations and subtractions in geometric proofs.
